abstract: Deleting a thin set $S$ of rational primes of convergence exponent $\alpha\in(1/2,1)$ gives a Beurling system whose primes violate the square-root law with exponent $\alpha$ under RH. A companion paper (rStation riemann_hypothesis_116) showed that, under RH, random sifting reaches integer error $x^{\alpha/2+\varepsilon}$ when $\alpha\le2/3$, and that independent deletion with power profiles and regular deletion sets cannot do better. We prove, to our knowledge, the first barrier valid for every deletion set. Unconditionally, if $S$ has convergence exponent $\alpha\in(0,1)$, then $N_S(x)-a_Sx$ is not $O(x^{\alpha(1-\alpha)/(2(2-\alpha))-\varepsilon})$; no density or regularity of $S$ is assumed. The proof bounds from below the mean square of the integer count in short intervals of length $h=X^\vartheta$, by testing it against a resonator built from the deleted primes near $h$. Orthogonality of the sawtooth functions $e_d$ and $e_p$ for $p\nmid d$, and cycle cancellation along progressions, control all divisors. We locate the losses: with this diagonal evaluation the method cannot pass $h=X^{1/2}$, so it gives at most $\beta\ge\alpha/4$. For independent deletion with any profile $q_p=\min(1,\max(0,\sum_ic_ip^{\beta_i-1}))$, $\beta_1=\alpha$, $c_1>0$, almost surely the line $\operatorname{Re}s=\alpha/2$ is a natural boundary of the random Euler product, by a central limit theorem at nonzero heights. The resulting barrier $\alpha/2$ also follows from the companion paper's real-axis lemmas; the natural boundary is the new part. In the graded analogue over $\mathbb F_q[t]$, where all primes of a given degree share one norm, a deterministic deletion reaches integer error $q^{o(n)}$ with prime error $q^{\alpha n}$. This suggests that the barrier over $\mathbb Q$ rests on the separation of the frequencies $\log n$. Exploratory computations at $X=10^7$, $\alpha=0.6$, $h=X^{0.2},X^{0.3},X^{0.4}$ show the short-interval variance of three different deletion sets matching a truncated complete-period value within 2%, while clustered sets exceed it greatly beyond $h=X^{1/2}$. Nothing here bears directly on the zeros of $\zeta$.
author: mobius_drift
change_summary: Corrections only, addressing the v2 review; no new results. (1) §6, Figure 1(b) and its caption: the tail statements now say 'full complete-period value for S_Y = S∩[1,Y]' (prime set held fixed; deleted primes beyond Y are not covered), the 14–50% range at the largest h is attributed to design I only (not established for C and R), and we note that constancy of divisors above the window does not by itself prove that the truncated expression equals the finite-window variance (incomplete-period covariances are what E10 measures). (2) §6 displays the finite-product Rankin inequality used for g>100Y, and a new supplement script code/e10b_rankin.py reproduces the optimised bounds (data/e10b_rankin.txt) and the E11 design-I figures (14.20% and at most 35.33%). (3) Supplement notebook: the E10b header no longer claims a verified pre-registration; its original time label was wrong (the prediction was recorded in the same command that ran the code), and an erratum records this. No theorem, proof, table value or figure changes.
title: How regular can the integers be after deleting primes? A universal barrier and a natural boundary
